content: Write a cover letter for a marketing coordinator role at a nonprofit.

Here's a cover letter you can adapt. I've used brackets for the details only you can fill in — swap those out and adjust the accomplishments to match your real experience.

---

**[Your Name]**
[City, State] • [Phone] • [Email] • [LinkedIn or portfolio URL]

[Date]

[Hiring Manager Name]
[Title]
[Organization Name]
[Address]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

When I read that [Organization Name] was hiring a Marketing Coordinator, I was drawn in by [specific detail — a recent campaign, a program, an annual report stat, something from their site]. [One sentence on why that resonates with you personally or professionally.] I'd be glad to bring [X years] of marketing experience to a team doing that work.

In my current role as [Your Title] at [Current/Recent Employer], I manage the day-to-day execution of our marketing calendar across email, social, and web. A few things I've contributed:

- Grew our email list from [X] to [Y] subscribers in [timeframe] by [tactic], while maintaining an average open rate of [Z]%.
- Coordinated marketing for [event or campaign name], which [result — drove 300 registrations, raised $45K, doubled volunteer sign-ups].
- Built a content workflow that cut turnaround time on [deliverable] from [X] to [Y], giving our small team more room for planning instead of scrambling.

I'm comfortable being the person who does a bit of everything — writing the newsletter, sizing the graphic, pulling the analytics, and chasing down the program staff for a quote before deadline. My toolkit includes [Mailchimp/Constant Contact], [Canva/Adobe Creative Suite], [WordPress/Squarespace], [Salesforce/Bloomerang/HubSpot], and [Google Analytics/Meta Business Suite].

What draws me to nonprofit marketing specifically is that the work has a clear point. [One or two sentences: relevant volunteer work, lived experience with the issue area, a past nonprofit role, or why this mission matters to you. Be genuine and brief — this is often the paragraph hiring managers remember.]

I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I can support [Organization Name]'s [communications goals / upcoming campaign / growth]. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

---

**A few tips as you customize:**

- **Replace the bullets with your real numbers.** Even modest metrics ("grew Instagram engagement 18%") beat vague claims. If you don't have numbers, describe scope instead: "managed content for a 12,000-person subscriber list."
- **The mission paragraph matters more here than in corporate applications.** Nonprofits screen for people who won't leave in eight months. Be specific and honest rather than effusive.
- **Find a real name if you can** — check the org's staff page or LinkedIn. "Dear Hiring Committee" is a fine fallback; avoid "To Whom It May Concern."
- **Mirror their language.** If the posting says "storytelling" or "constituent engagement," use those words.
- **Keep it to one page** — around 300–400 words is plenty.

If you share the job posting and a bit about your background, I can tailor this into a specific draft for you.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

I've assumed "already knows the background" means the hiring manager knows *you* — you've volunteered there, interned, worked a contract, or come in through a strong internal referral. That changes a lot: you can skip the mission-fit pitch and the resume recap, and instead write like someone continuing a conversation.

---

**[Your Name]**
[City, State] • [Phone] • [Email]

[Date]

Dear [First Name],

I'm applying for the Marketing Coordinator role, and since you already know most of what a cover letter usually covers, I'll use this to say what the application itself can't.

The [volunteer work / contract / internship] I've done with [Organization] over the past [timeframe] has been the clearest test of whether this is work I want to do full time, and the answer is yes. [One specific moment — the week you rebuilt the newsletter template, the event you ran comms for, the conversation with a program director that reframed how you write about the work.] That's the part of the job I want more of.

A few things I'd want to take on in the role, based on what I've seen from the inside:

- **[Specific gap or opportunity you've noticed]** — [what you'd do about it, in one line]. I've already [drafted / tested / started] [something concrete], and I'd want to finish it properly.
- **[Second one]** — [approach].
- **[Third one, ideally something that helps the team, not just the metrics]** — e.g., documenting the content workflow so it survives staff turnover.

I know the constraints here: [small team / limited budget / competing priorities across programs]. I'd rather do three things consistently than announce ten. My instinct is to start by [first 90 days in one sentence].

Happy to talk through any of this whenever it's useful. Thanks for the encouragement to apply — [or: thanks for thinking of me for this].

[Your Name]

---

**What changed and why:**

- **No mission paragraph.** They know why you care; restating it reads as filler or, worse, as if you forgot they know you.
- **No skills list.** They've seen your work. Listing Mailchimp to someone who watched you use Mailchimp is a downgrade.
- **Forward-looking, not backward.** With a cold reader you prove you *can* do the job. With a warm reader you show what you'd *do with* the job. The middle section becomes a mini-plan rather than a highlight reel.
- **Shorter and less formal.** Roughly 250 words. The stiff register of a standard cover letter would land oddly from someone they've had coffee with.
- **Acknowledges constraints.** Insider credibility comes from knowing what's hard, not from enthusiasm.

**One caution:** if the role goes through a formal HR process or a hiring committee, other people may read this who *don't* know you. In that case, add one sentence up top establishing your history — "As you know, I've coordinated communications for [Program] as a volunteer since [year]" — so the letter still works for a stranger.

If you meant a different reader — a board member, a former colleague at another org, someone who knows the *organization* but not you — tell me which and I'll redo it.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

Assuming this is for an email body or an application-form text box — places where a formatted letter looks out of place and people skim. I kept the warm-reader framing and cut to about 125 words.

---

**Subject: Marketing Coordinator — [Your Name]**

Hi [First Name],

I'm applying for the Marketing Coordinator role, and I'd want to spend the first few months on three things: [opportunity #1], [opportunity #2], and documenting the content workflow so it doesn't live in one person's head.

Those come from what I've seen [volunteering / contracting] here since [year] — including [one specific project in four or five words]. I know the constraints, and I'd rather do a few things consistently than announce ten.

Résumé attached. Happy to talk whenever it's useful.

[Your Name]
[Phone] • [Email]

---

**What I cut and why:**

- **The "since you already know the background" opener.** Clever framing costs a sentence you no longer have. Lead with the plan.
- **The specific-moment anecdote.** It was the emotional core of the longer version, but at this length the concrete plan does more work.
- **The bulleted list.** Three items in a sentence read faster on a phone than three bullets with sub-clauses.
- **The 90-day line.** It was redundant once the plan moved to the top.

What survived: the plan, the proof you've been inside, and the constraint acknowledgment. Those are the three things a warm reader can't get from your résumé.

**If the placement is different than I guessed:**

- **LinkedIn message** — drop the subject line and "Résumé attached," add "I've applied through the portal."
- **Form field with a hard character limit** — cut the second paragraph to just "This comes from [volunteering] here since [year]."
- **Still a formal letter, just shorter** — say so and I'll restore the salutation and sign-off block.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

Heads up before the revision: this version doesn't contain a quantified results claim — the metrics dropped out back when we cut the bullets. The closest thing is the project reference in paragraph two, which implies a track record without stating an outcome. I've removed that, since it's the likeliest thing you meant. Everything else is untouched.

---

**Subject: Marketing Coordinator — [Your Name]**

Hi [First Name],

I'm applying for the Marketing Coordinator role, and I'd want to spend the first few months on three things: [opportunity #1], [opportunity #2], and documenting the content workflow so it doesn't live in one person's head.

Those come from what I've seen [volunteering / contracting] here since [year]. I know the constraints, and I'd rather do a few things consistently than announce ten.

Résumé attached. Happy to talk whenever it's useful.

[Your Name]
[Phone] • [Email]

---

**One tradeoff to be aware of:** that clause was the only evidence of what you've actually done here. What's left establishes that you've been around since [year], which still supports the plan — but if the reader is anyone other than the person who knows your work directly, the letter now leans entirely on the résumé for proof.

**If I guessed wrong,** the other candidate is "I'd rather do a few things consistently than announce ten" — a claim about how you work rather than about outcomes, but it does gesture at reliability. Say the word and I'll cut that instead, or both.
